title: Stiffness, Strength, and Stability
description: Practice questions on stiffness, strength, serviceability, structural efficiency, vibration, and stability.

questions.question: When a design is limited by stiffness rather than strength, which material property is the primary driver for material selection?
questions.explanation: Stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation. Young's modulus governs elastic strain and deflection, whereas yield and ultimate strengths govern failure limits.

questions.question: For a long, slender column under axial compression, a stability failure occurs when:

choices.A: The internal stress exceeds the yield strength.
choices.B: A small disturbance produces large unintended displacements.
choices.C: The part permanently deforms without fracture.
choices.D: The vibration frequency equals the natural frequency.

questions.explanation: Stability concerns the ability of an equilibrium configuration to recover after a small disturbance. Buckling is the common example.

questions.question: A precision optical bench must not deflect more than 1 micron under its own weight. This is primarily a requirement for:
questions.explanation: The component is not necessarily yielding or buckling; it is limited by allowable elastic deformation, which is a stiffness or serviceability requirement.

questions.question: If a beam material is changed from low-carbon steel to a high-strength heat-treated alloy steel, how does the beam stiffness change if the geometry remains unchanged?

choices.A: It increases significantly because yield strength is higher.
choices.B: It remains essentially unchanged because Young's modulus is nearly the same.
choices.C: It decreases because higher-strength materials are usually more brittle.
choices.D: It depends on the factor of safety.

questions.explanation: Heat treatment can substantially increase strength, but it has little effect on Young's modulus. Therefore, beams of the same geometry made from common steels have nearly the same elastic deflection.

questions.question: A thin-walled cylinder under external pressure collapses inward while its hoop stress is well below yield. This is a failure in:
questions.explanation: Thin-walled shells can lose geometric stability and collapse at stresses far below the material yield strength.

questions.question: Which change increases bending stiffness through geometry without changing material volume?

choices.A: Use a solid shaft instead of a hollow shaft of the same weight.
choices.B: Increase the depth of an I-beam while reducing flange thickness.
choices.C: Polish the surface to remove stress risers.
choices.D: Use a material with a higher yield strength.

questions.explanation: Bending stiffness depends on EI. Redistributing material farther from the neutral axis increases the area moment of inertia without necessarily adding material.

questions.question: A bridge is strong enough not to collapse but sways excessively in the wind and makes pedestrians uncomfortable. Which design criterion has failed?
questions.explanation: Excessive elastic motion or vibration is a serviceability problem associated with insufficient stiffness.

questions.question: For an elastic Euler column, the critical buckling load is independent of:
questions.explanation: Euler buckling depends on E, I, effective length, and end conditions. Yield strength does not appear as long as buckling remains elastic.

questions.question: In design for strength, the primary objective is to ensure that:

choices.B: Maximum stress remains below the allowable stress.
choices.D: The Euler load is not exceeded.

questions.explanation: Strength design compares stress demand with an allowable material strength, usually including a factor of safety.

questions.question: Which failure mode is characterized by a bifurcation point in the load-deflection curve?
questions.explanation: At the critical load, a perfectly straight configuration can lose stability and branch into a buckled equilibrium path.

questions.question: If the span of a simply supported beam is doubled while the load and cross-section remain unchanged, its bending stiffness decreases by approximately what factor?
questions.explanation: For common simply supported beam loading, deflection scales with L^3. Since stiffness is load divided by deflection, stiffness scales with 1/L^3.

questions.question: A material has a high strength-to-weight ratio but a low stiffness-to-weight ratio. It is most likely:
questions.explanation: Some polymers and composites can carry relatively high stress for their weight while still having a comparatively low elastic modulus.

questions.question: Notch sensitivity is important in design for _____ but is usually negligible in design for _____.
questions.explanation: Notches amplify local stress and strongly affect fatigue crack initiation, but a small notch usually has little effect on the global section stiffness.

questions.question: Why does a fixed-fixed column have a higher critical buckling load than a pinned-pinned column of the same material and geometry?

choices.A: It has a higher yield strength.
choices.C: Its Young's modulus increases because of the restraints.
choices.D: Its internal stresses are always lower.

questions.explanation: End restraints reduce the effective buckling length, and the Euler critical load varies inversely with the square of effective length.

questions.question: Why is stiffness important in the design of a high-speed rotating shaft?

choices.A: It directly sets the torque at yielding.
choices.B: It influences the critical speeds and natural frequencies.
choices.C: It determines bearing fatigue life by itself.

questions.explanation: Shaft stiffness affects the system's natural frequencies. Operation near a critical speed can produce severe whirling and vibration.

questions.question: A short column usually fails by _____, whereas a long slender column usually fails by _____.
questions.explanation: Stocky columns tend to reach material strength limits, while slender columns are governed by elastic or inelastic buckling.

questions.question: Flexural rigidity is defined as:
questions.explanation: Flexural rigidity combines the material modulus E and the cross-sectional bending property I.

questions.question: Why is aeroelasticity a concern in aircraft-wing design?

choices.A: It involves interaction between aerodynamic loading and structural stiffness that can cause flutter.
choices.B: It concerns only the weight of the wing.
choices.C: It ensures the wing is strong enough to support the engines.
choices.D: It is concerned only with surface finish.

questions.explanation: Aeroelastic flutter is a dynamic instability caused by interaction among aerodynamic forces, structural stiffness, inertia, and damping.

questions.question: For a statically indeterminate structure, calculation of the reactions requires knowledge of the structure's:
questions.explanation: Equilibrium alone is insufficient. Compatibility equations and force-deformation relations are needed.

questions.question: Which statement is false?

choices.A: A part can be strong enough but not stiff enough.
choices.B: A part can be stiff enough but not strong enough.
choices.C: A part that buckles must have reached its yield strength.
choices.D: Geometry strongly influences stiffness and stability.

questions.explanation: A sufficiently slender member can buckle elastically at a stress below yield.

questions.question: Two beams have identical bending stiffness but different strengths. Which statement is consistent with this observation?

choices.A: They must use the same material but different geometries.
choices.B: They may use different materials or geometries but have the same EI.
choices.C: They must have identical yield strength.
choices.D: They must have identical cross-sectional area.

questions.explanation: Bending stiffness is governed by EI. Different combinations of E and I can yield the same stiffness while strength remains different.

questions.question: A design is limited by deflection under variable loading. Which consideration becomes especially important?
questions.explanation: Under variable loading, stiffness affects vibration, resonance, and dynamic amplification in addition to static deflection.

questions.question: Why does increasing the depth of a beam improve bending stiffness more effectively than increasing its width?

choices.B: The area moment of inertia scales nonlinearly with depth.

questions.explanation: For a rectangular section, I = bh^3/12, so depth has a cubic influence while width has a linear influence.

questions.question: A structure undergoes a large deformation but returns to its original shape after unloading. This most directly indicates:
questions.explanation: Full recovery indicates elastic behavior. The large deformation suggests insufficient stiffness for the intended service requirement.

questions.question: Why is increasing material strength often ineffective for improving the elastic buckling resistance of a slender member?

choices.A: Buckling depends primarily on geometry and elastic stiffness.

questions.explanation: Elastic buckling load is governed by EI and effective length, not directly by yield strength.

questions.question: Why is stiffness often more restrictive than strength in lightweight design?

choices.B: Deflection limits can be reached before stress limits.

questions.explanation: In many lightweight structures, stress is acceptable while deflection, vibration, or alignment requirements govern the design.

questions.question: Which design change can improve bending stiffness without increasing mass?

choices.B: Redistribute material farther from the neutral axis.

questions.explanation: Moving material away from the neutral axis increases I and therefore EI without necessarily adding mass.

questions.question: A column is shortened while all other properties remain unchanged. Which behavior improves most strongly?
questions.explanation: Euler buckling load scales with 1/L^2, so reducing length strongly increases resistance to buckling.

questions.question: Why are thin-walled structural sections often efficient for bending stiffness?

choices.B: They place material far from the neutral axis.
choices.D: They always reduce stress to zero.

questions.explanation: Thin-walled sections can achieve a large moment of inertia by distributing material far from the centroid with relatively little mass.

questions.question: What is the principal trade-off when stiffness is increased simply by adding material?
questions.explanation: Adding material generally increases stiffness but also increases mass, which may be undesirable in transportation and aerospace applications.

questions.question: A structure designed only to satisfy stiffness requirements may still fail because of:

choices.C: A reduction in modulus caused by calculation

questions.explanation: Adequate stiffness does not guarantee adequate strength. Stress must also remain below applicable material limits.

questions.question: Why do ribs improve the stiffness of a panel?

choices.A: They increase the material's yield strength.
choices.B: They increase the effective moment of inertia with relatively little added mass.
choices.D: They change the material's Young's modulus.

questions.explanation: Ribs redistribute material away from the neutral surface and increase geometric stiffness efficiently.

questions.question: Which scenario most clearly indicates a stability-driven failure rather than a strength-driven failure?

choices.B: Sudden lateral deflection under compressive load

questions.explanation: Sudden lateral deflection under compression is characteristic of buckling, a loss of structural stability.

questions.question: Why are boundary conditions critical in a stability analysis?

choices.B: They alter effective length, deformation modes, and buckling behavior.
choices.D: They always change the applied load magnitude.

questions.explanation: Support restraints determine admissible buckling shapes and effective length, which directly influence critical load.

questions.question: A component has acceptable stress but excessive vibration. This most directly indicates:
questions.explanation: Low dynamic stiffness can lead to resonance or excessive vibration even when stress remains acceptable.

questions.question: Why is simply increasing cross-sectional area not always the most efficient way to improve bending stiffness?

choices.B: The added material may not be placed where it efficiently increases the moment of inertia.

questions.explanation: Bending stiffness depends not only on material quantity but also on how far that material is located from the neutral axis.

questions.question: Why is the load path important in stiffness design?

choices.A: It determines the material yield strength.
choices.B: It affects how forces and deformation are distributed through the structure.

questions.explanation: A direct and efficient load path limits localized bending and deformation, whereas a poor load path can create flexible regions.

questions.question: Why are arches efficient structural forms?

choices.B: They convert much of the loading into axial compression.

questions.explanation: Arches carry loads largely through compression, reducing bending moments and improving structural efficiency.

questions.question: How does local buckling differ from global buckling?

choices.A: It depends only on material strength.
choices.B: It occurs in localized thin elements or regions.
choices.C: It always requires a higher load.

questions.explanation: Local buckling involves individual plates, flanges, webs, or shell regions, whereas global buckling involves the member or structure as a whole.

questions.question: A design must satisfy stiffness, strength, and stability simultaneously. Which requirement governs the final design?

choices.A: The requirement with the highest numerical factor of safety
choices.C: The material with the highest modulus

questions.explanation: All criteria must be satisfied, but the limiting or most restrictive criterion controls the final dimensions and material choice.
